Enjoy it? I mean, maybe for the first bite or two, but honestly, no, I don't really taste it after that. It's just... I'm just shoveling it in, you know? It's not about enjoying a good meal. 

Speaking of a good meal, though, you ever had proper Texas brisket? Wasted a good thirty-dollar piece of meat trying to figure it out before I just gave up and threw some hot dogs on the regular grill.

Well, it's pretty much an every week thing. Most weeks I'll have at least one night where I just eat like that, completely out of control, and then I have to figure out how to undo it, you know? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, my weight goes up and down a little, but I watch it like a hawk. Even when my work pants feel looser, if I step on the scale and it's up even a single pound, I just panic. I feel like I'm getting fat and I start worrying I'm going to lose control of my whole body, you know? It's terrifying. 

Speaking of losing control of your body, you ever see a guy try to lift a transmission without a proper jack? Man, I saw this kid, new hire at the shop, trying to muscle a heavy-duty Allison transmission onto a workbench all by himself. Those things weigh, like, six, seven hundred pounds easy. I yelled at him to stop, but he already had it halfway up. Next thing you know, his knees buckle, the transmission slips, and he goes down hard. Pinned his leg right under the bell housing. We had to get three guys and a pry bar just to get it off him. He ended up fracturing his tibia in two places. Out on worker's comp for three months. I told the boss, I said, you gotta train these kids better. You can't just throw them in the bay and expect them to know how to use the equipment. We got transmission jacks for a reason! They're on wheels, they got safety chains, you just pump the handle and it does all the work. But no, this kid wanted to be Superman. Now he's walking with a limp and probably will for the rest of his life. It's just stupid, you know? You gotta use the right tools for the job. 

But yeah, the weight thing... if the scale goes up even a pound, I just lose it. I feel like I'm getting huge and everything is spiraling out of control.

I just feel gross and tired.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating during those episodes?\n\nPatient: Like I was saying a minute ago, no, I don't have any control at all. Man, it is the most terrifying thing. We had this old Cummins come into the shop a few months back, and the seals on the turbo were completely shot. It started sucking its own engine oil into the intake and burning it as fuel. When that happens, turning the ignition key off does absolutely nothing. Well, it's... I guess I'd say I do it sometimes. After I eat way too much on those nights, I usually end up going to the bathroom to make myself throw up, or sometimes I'll take a bunch of laxatives. I don't know if you know much about modern diesel emissions systems, but the SCR catalyst is incredibly sensitive. You put anything other than pure urea and deionized water in there, and you're looking at a catastrophic failure. I mean, we're talking a five, maybe six thousand dollar repair bill if that washer fluid hits the injector and bakes onto the catalyst. The guy was practically in tears when he saw the bill, but I told him, buddy, you're lucky you didn't start the engine. If that stuff had cycled through the system, you'd be buying a whole new exhaust setup.

Not always, no. Sometimes... well, after a bad night of eating, I’ll just skip breakfast and lunch at work the next day. Or I’ll push myself through extra runs and a bunch of push-ups, even when I’m completely worn out from being on my feet all day.

I told the shop manager we need anti-fatigue mats in the heavy bays, but you know how cheap management is. They won't spend a dime unless it makes them a dollar. But yeah, anyway, even after a grueling shift like that, if I messed up and ate too much the night before, I'll still force myself to go run or do the push-ups. I just skip the meals and grind it out, no matter how dead my legs feel.

No, I don't think I ever just... leave it alone. Most weeks I have at least one night where I eat like that, just a ton of food, and then I always try to make up for it somehow—throwing up, taking laxatives, skipping meals, or working out extra. It’s been going on for several months now. I just can't let it sit there. 

It’s kind of like when someone ignores a maintenance issue, you know? You can't just pretend it's not there. We had this guy bring in a Freightliner Cascadia a while back, running a Detroit DD15 engine. He knew he had a slow coolant leak. He could see the reservoir dropping, but instead of fixing the root cause, he just kept driving it. Said he was on a tight schedule and didn't have time for downtime. Well, the coolant was leaking internally, right into the oil. If you know anything about heavy-duty engines, coolant and oil make this nasty, milky sludge that completely destroys your lubrication. 

He drove it like that for weeks. Finally, the main bearings just gave out. He spun a bearing going 65 down the interstate and threw a rod right through the side of the engine block. A fifty-dollar gasket leak turned into a thirty-thousand-dollar total engine replacement just because he didn't deal with what was happening inside the system. I spent three whole days just pulling the shattered pieces of that block out of the chassis. The smell of burnt oil and baked antifreeze... man, it is something you never get out of your clothes. I wash my work uniforms separate from my regular clothes, but I swear, my truck still smells like it sometimes. I had to buy these special heavy-duty ozone generators just to get the stench out of the cab of my own pickup... 

But, uh, anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right. Yeah, no, I never just eat all that and do nothing. I always have to make up for it.

Wasted a good thirty-dollar piece of meat trying to figure it out before I just gave up and threw some hot dogs on the regular grill. \n\nBut yeah, the food when I'm eating like that... no, I don't really taste it or enjoy it. The things were practically solid black when I pulled them out. And he was wondering why he was losing power on the hills! You're talking a couple grand just for the part, not to mention the labor. \n\nBut yeah, the eating thing... at least once a week, and then I do whatever I can to get rid of it. It's like my brain just switches off and I'm just doing it. \n\nKind of like when you're driving a familiar route, you know? You ever do that? Where you drive all the way home from work and you pull into the driveway and you realize you don't even remember the last five miles? Highway hypnosis, they call it. Nothing to look at but concrete barriers and the occasional dead deer. I took this Kenworth T680 out last Tuesday—guy said he had a vibration in the steering column at exactly 65 miles an hour. Which, let me tell you, is the most annoying kind of problem to diagnose. Because it could be anything. Could be a tire out of balance, could be a worn kingpin, could be a U-joint starting to go bad on the driveshaft. So I get it up to 65, and sure enough, there's this tiny little shimmy. Some of these guys, they rely too much on the service brakes instead of using the engine brake. Jake brakes are loud, sure, but they save your pads and rotors. \n\nBut yeah, the eating... I don't think it's always an emotional thing. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that. Control? No, not at all. Honestly, once I start on those bad nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food, you know? Like, I'm literally inside my head telling myself to stop, and I’m already feeling physically sick from how much I've had, but I just can't make myself quit. 

It’s like I can't shut the system down once it starts feeding itself. It actually reminds me exactly of a diesel runaway. Have you ever heard of that? It’s probably the most terrifying thing that can happen in a shop. 

See, diesel engines don't use spark plugs like a gas car; they run purely on compression. So if a turbocharger seal blows and starts leaking engine oil into the air intake, the engine will start burning its own motor oil as fuel. You can turn the ignition key completely off, pull it right out of the dash, and the engine will just keep accelerating on its own. It just feeds on itself and you have absolutely zero control over it. The RPMs go way past the redline, the block starts shaking, it sounds like a jet engine about to explode, and the whole shop instantly fills with this thick, blinding white smoke. 

We had an old International box truck do that last summer. The driver brought it in complaining about a weird whistle, and my buddy Dave fired it up in the bay, and bam—instant runaway. The only way to stop it is to completely choke off the air supply. Dave was running around screaming for a piece of plywood or a thick clipboard to slap over the turbo intake. You can't use your hand, because the suction is so strong it'll literally pull your fingers off. We finally jammed a heavy Chilton repair manual over the pipe and it choked out just before the connecting rods decided to launch themselves through the oil pan. Man, my heart was beating out of my chest. 

But, uh... yeah. That feeling where you turn the key off, you know you need to stop, but the engine just keeps screaming anyway? That's... that's kind of what it feels like when I'm eating. I'm telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going.

It's terrifying. \n\nSpeaking of losing control of your body, you ever see a guy try to lift a transmission without a proper jack? Man, I saw this kid, new hire at the shop, trying to muscle a heavy-duty Allison transmission onto a workbench all by himself. Those things weigh, like, six, seven hundred pounds easy. I yelled at him to stop, but he already had it halfway up. Next thing you know, his knees buckle, the transmission slips, and he goes down hard. Pinned his leg right under the bell housing. We had to get three guys and a pry bar just to get it off him. He ended up fracturing his tibia in two places. Out on worker's comp for three months. I told the boss, I said, you gotta train these kids better. You can't just throw them in the bay and expect them to know how to use the equipment. We got transmission jacks for a reason! They're on wheels, they got safety chains, you just pump the handle and it does all the work. But no, this kid wanted to be Superman. Now he's walking with a limp and probably will for the rest of his life. It's just stupid, you know? You gotta use the right tools for the job. \n\nBut yeah, the weight thing... if the scale goes up even a pound, I just lose it. I feel like I'm getting huge and everything is spiraling out of control.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel bad about yourself after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I do. I feel really disgusted with myself, honestly. Like, I just sit there looking at all the empty wrappers and containers and I just feel so ashamed. It's like, how could I let this happen again, you know? \n\nIt's that same kind of sick feeling you get when you realize you messed up a repair and the customer's already on the road. We had this fleet contract a couple years back, servicing these Peterbilt 389s for a local logging company. Beautiful trucks, classic long-nose style, but they run them hard out in the woods. Mud, rocks, steep grades, you name it. Anyway, I was doing a routine brake job on one of the trailers, replacing the shoes and turning the drums. I thought I had everything buttoned up tight, torqued the lug nuts to spec, the whole nine yards. But I must have gotten distracted, maybe by one of the other guys asking for a tool, because I completely forgot to reinstall the cotter pin on the main slack adjuster clevis. \n\nSo the driver takes the rig out, gets fully loaded with timber, and starts heading down this nasty 6% grade. He hits the brakes, and because that pin was missing, the clevis slips right off. Suddenly he's got zero braking power on that axle. He had to ride the engine brake so hard he almost blew the turbo, and he ended up having to take a runaway truck ramp just to stop the thing. Buried the front end up to the bumper in gravel. When the boss found out it was my bay that truck came out of... man, I felt lower than dirt. I couldn't even look him in the eye. Cost the shop thousands in towing and repairs, not to mention almost getting the driver killed. I didn't sleep for a week after that, just kept replaying it in my head. Man, I remember this one time, we had a guy bring in his F-350, one of those newer ones with the 6.7 Powerstroke. Beautiful rig, lifted, custom exhaust, the works. Anyway, he accidentally topped off his DEF tank—the diesel exhaust fluid—with standard windshield washer fluid. Just poured a whole gallon of the blue stuff right in there. \n\nI don't know if you know much about modern diesel emissions systems, but the SCR catalyst is incredibly sensitive. You put anything other than pure urea and deionized water in there, and you're looking at a catastrophic failure. I mean, we're talking a five, maybe six thousand dollar repair bill if that washer fluid hits the injector and bakes onto the catalyst. I was siphoning that tank like my life depended on it, trying to get every last drop of that blue garbage out of there. We ended up having to drop the whole tank, flush the lines, replace the DEF pump and the heater assembly just to be safe. It was a nightmare. The guy was practically in tears when he saw the bill, but I told him, buddy, you're lucky you didn't start the engine. If that stuff had cycled through the system, you'd be buying a whole new exhaust setup. \n\nBut yeah, that panic... that need to just purge the system before the damage is done.
